newsitem.title: ITALY: Bank Italy not seen pushing for early ERM entry.
newsitem.headline: Bank Italy not seen pushing for early ERM entry.

text.p: The Bank of Italy is sceptical about the benefits of an early return of the lira to the European Exchange Rate Mechanism, according to an interview with central bank governor Antonio Fazio in Saturday's Corriere della Sera newspaper.
But while the Bank appears less than favourable to a return to the grid it left in a wave of currency turbulence in September 1992, the governor made clear the decision was up to the government.
Romano Prodi, prime minister of the centre-left administration which came to power in April general elections, has made an early return to the ERM a main priority.

"I understand the political problem, but on a strictly monetary level I note that if we had rejoined the ERM straight after the currency crisis, the lira/mark exchange rate probably would be around the 1200 lire level," said Fazio.
"Instead, in little over a year we have succeeded, being outside the system, to manage in as stable manner a 20 percent revaluation of the lira... a phenomenon of this size not seen since 1947.
"I wonder how useful it is to return now to an exchange rate pact which, having such broad links as the 15 percent band, has lost much of its significance," Fazio said.

The Corriere added that the Bank of Italy regarded sterling as a more "European" currency which, although kept out of the grid by London, does not fluctuate more than 3-4 percent against the mark with respect to currencies remaining within the grid which use the fluctuation margins to a huge extent.
On the state of the Italian economy, apart from high deficits, Fazio was far from pessimistic as he noted most of the fundamentals were positive, although growth in gross domestic product was low.
"This year we will see (GDP growth) of between 0.5 and 1.1 percent", and there was the serious problem of unemployment.
"But these problems could only be tackled with a healthy economy. And today we have a strong trade surplus, comparable only with that of Japan, while currency reserves are at the level of Germany's."

He noted that the spread between Italian bonds and German bunds had narrowed from a high of around 650 basis points to some 300 bps despite the fact the Bank of Italy had kept its key discount rate unchanged at a high 9.0 percent until July's cut to 8.25 percent.
The Bank's tight monetary policy, much criticised by politicians, unions and industry, had paid off, Fazio said.
He said this was because it had convinced the markets that Italy was serious in its battle against inflation, with CPI at 3.4 percent year on year in August showing a seventh consecutive fall.
